info.name: API Workshop - Procurement Invoices
info.description:
Hands-on API workshop: connection, data structure, pagination,
flattening, and error handling.

GETTING STARTED
1. Pick the 'Workshop API (local)' environment, top right.
2. Open folder 1 and run C1.
3. That is it -- the bearer token is fetched automatically and
   refreshed when it expires. You never paste a token by hand.

Requests whose names say '-> 422' or '-> 503' are SUPPOSED to fail.
Their descriptions explain what to look for.

Every request has a description. Read them: they are the workbook.

exec: // Fetches a bearer token automatically, so every request just works after
// import. Skips itself for the token endpoint, and reuses a token that is
// still valid for at least another minute.

item.name: 1. Connection (C1-C3)
item.description: Reach the API, get a token, then prove the token works. Do these in order.

request.description:
Is the API reachable at all? No token needed.

If this fails, it is a network problem, not an auth problem:
  - wrong host or port
  - http:// vs https://
  - a proxy or VPN in the way
  - on Azure, a 20-30s cold start on the very first call

Check app_version / git_commit / uptime_seconds in the body to
confirm which deployment you're actually talking to. A restart
resets uptime_seconds and re-runs the seed, so data and logins
come back exactly as before -- but expect a few extra seconds
on the very next request while that happens.

This SHOULD fail with 422. It is here on purpose.

The endpoint expects form-encoded fields, not JSON. Read the
error body: it tells you username and password are missing --
because the server never looked in the JSON body for them.

Now compare with C2b.

exec: pm.test('complains the fields are missing', function () {

request.description:
The same credentials, sent as x-www-form-urlencoded. This works.

The token is saved to the environment automatically, so every
other request in this collection can use it.

No Authorization header at all -> 403 Forbidden.

Compare with C3b, which sends a *bad* token and gets 401.
Two different codes for two different situations:
  403 = you did not present credentials
  401 = you presented credentials and they were rejected

Many people expect these the other way around. Worth a think.
A syntactically fine but invalid token -> 401 Unauthorized.

Who am I, and when does my token expire?

token_expires_in_seconds is the useful one: if requests suddenly
start returning 401 mid-session, check here first.

item.name: 2. Data structure (D1-D2)
item.description: Both requests here hit the two XML-only endpoints (see Part 2 -- Data Structure): the response body is XML, not JSON, even though D2's request body stays JSON. An error on either (a 404, a 422) still comes back as the standard JSON error envelope -- only the successful data body is XML.

item.name: D1  GET /v1/invoices/{number}  one fully nested invoice (XML)

request.description:
One invoice, fully expanded. This is the shape you will flatten.

The response is XML, not JSON (see WHAT IS XML? in 02_data_structure.py).
Check the Content-Type header, and look at the body: it is an
<invoice> document, with <line_items><item>...</item></line_items>
and <postings><item>...</item></postings> nested inside -- 'item' is
the repeated-child convention for every list.

Map the nesting and mark the cardinality of each level:
  invoice -> line_items[] -> postings[]

Note vendor_number is a plain field on the invoice, NOT a nested
object -- resolving it to a name/address means calling
GET /v1/master-data/vendors separately.

GET vs POST, made concrete: this is GET because the whole filter is
one simple thing -- an invoice number -- that fits cleanly into the
URL path itself. No body at all. Compare with D2.

A 404 on this same endpoint still comes back as the standard JSON
error envelope (see E1c) -- only the success body is XML.

The same nesting as D1, but wrapped in a paginated envelope -- and
again, the response is XML, not JSON.

The envelope is <invoice_search_response> wrapping <data>, <page>,
and <meta>, same three-part shape as the JSON version just spelled
out in tags instead of keys. The rows are in <data> -- not at the
top level.

GET vs POST, made concrete: this is still a READ (200, nothing
created, safe to repeat), exactly like D1 -- but the filter here
(page_size, an optional cursor, and in a real call vendor/account/
date filters too) is too structured to cram into a URL safely. So
it moves into a JSON body, and the method becomes POST even though
nothing is being created. Compare with D1: same kind of operation,
different method, because the shape of the input differs.

item.name: 3. Pagination (P1-P4)
item.description:
Two different pagination styles, one per endpoint -- because you will meet both in the wild. Master data uses limit/offset (P1). Invoice search uses cursors (P2).

P3 and P4 are ground-truth reference calls for two debugging exercises in VS Code (training/starters/03a_pagination_offset.py and 03b_pagination_cursor.py) -- each of those scripts runs, drifts (duplicates and/or an undercount), and you fix a one-line bug.

request.description:
Is the API reachable at all? No token needed.

If this fails, it is a network problem, not an auth problem:
  - wrong host or port
  - http:// vs https://
  - a proxy or VPN in the way
  - on Azure, a 20-30s cold start on the very first call

Check app_version / git_commit / uptime_seconds in the body to
confirm which deployment you're actually talking to. A restart
resets uptime_seconds and re-runs the seed, so data and logins
come back exactly as before -- but expect a few extra seconds
on the very next request while that happens.

Offset pagination -- you control the window directly with two params:
  limit    how many rows to return (capped at 50 -- try limit=999 and
           you get 422, not a silently-capped response)
  offset   how many rows to skip from the start

Change offset to 5, then 10, then 15 and hit Send again each time --
watch the `page` object: `total` stays the same, but `returned` and
`next_offset` shift, and a different slice of vendor_numbers comes
back. Try offset=99999 too -- that is NOT an error: you get back 200
with an empty items array and has_more=false (no results is not the
same as something broke).

This request is pure demonstration -- nothing here is broken. P3 below
is where an offset bug produces visibly wrong results, fixed in VS Code
(training/starters/03a_pagination_offset.py), not here.

Cursor pagination -- the other style this API uses, on invoice search.
The request body below is still JSON -- only the RESPONSE is XML (see
Part 2 -- Data Structure). Note what the response's <page> element does
and does not contain:
  next_cursor      an opaque token for the next page
  estimated_total  present on page 1 ONLY

There is no page count, and no offset param to hand-pick a page --
the only way to get page 2 is to send back the exact next_cursor this
page gives you. Run P2b to do that.

The cursor is saved to {{next_cursor}} for you.

exec: console.log('(decode it: it is just base64 JSON)');

request.description:
Page 2, using the cursor P2a saved.

Look at estimated_total now. It is empty/null.

So you cannot compute total / page_size to know when to stop.
The only correct rule is: keep going until next_cursor is empty/null.
That is deliberate -- it is how most real cursor APIs behave.

exec: pm.test('estimated_total is empty/null on page 2', function () {

request.description:
Ground truth for the offset-pagination ticket you debug in VS Code
(training/starters/03a_pagination_offset.py).

Note page.total here -- that is exactly how many vendors your VS Code
script needs to end up with, each one appearing exactly once. If it
collects a different count, or any vendor_number twice, the bug in
that script is still live.

Ground truth for the cursor-pagination ticket you debug in VS Code
(training/starters/03b_pagination_cursor.py). The request body is
JSON; the response is XML (see Part 2 -- Data Structure).

Note estimated_total and next_cursor here. Your VS Code script should
end up collecting estimated_total invoices in total, each
invoice_number appearing exactly once. If it does not -- especially if
the same invoice_numbers keep repeating -- the bug in that script is
still live.

item.name: 4. Flatten to files (F1-F3)
item.description:
Save these two responses to disk, then switch to VS Code.

In Postman: Send, then the Save Response dropdown (top right of the
response pane) -> Save to a file. Put them in training/data/.

Pre-saved copies are already in training/data/samples/ if you would
rather not wait.

item.name: F1  master-data  limit=10   -> save as master_data_page1.json

request.description:
Save this response to training/data/master_data_page1.json

Flatten it to one row per vendor. This one is intentionally easy:
vendor master data is already flat -- no nested objects, no
arrays. `pd.json_normalize` on this needs nothing special.

Keep this response open for comparison once you get to F2/F3:
the invoice data is a completely different shape.

item.name: F2/F3  search  page_size=10  -> save as invoices_page1.xml

request.description:
Save this response to training/data/samples/invoices_page1.xml

The response is XML, not JSON (see Part 2 -- Data Structure) -- save
it with a .xml extension, not .json, so the saved file actually
matches its own content.

Then produce, in Python:
  F2  one row per line item  (carry the invoice header down)
  F3  one row per posting    (carry invoice AND line down)

Then reconcile -- but at the INVOICE level, not per line: every
invoice's postings must sum to exactly 0.00, the way a real
double-entry journal entry balances (expense + VAT, both debit,
against Vendor Payable, credit). It does balance -- if yours
doesn't, look at the dtype of your money column.

exec: console.log('So your three flat files should have exactly those row counts.');

item.name: 5. Error handling (E1-E3)
item.description: Every one of these fails on purpose. Read the bodies carefully.

item.name: E1a  two validation errors at once  -> 422

request.description:
page_size is 0, and accounting_date_to is BEFORE accounting_date_from.

The response names every offending field, with a dotted path.
Fix both from the error body alone, without reading source.

`limit` is not a thing here, and it is not silently ignored
either -- the error names the key it did not expect.

This is the single most common real mistake against a new API:
a valid-looking parameter at the wrong nesting level.
A /v1 404. Note the code, the request_id, and retryable=false.

Fails roughly every third call, per user, with 503 +
Retry-After: 2.

503 not 500, deliberately: this is transient and retrying is the
right response. Hit Send a few times and watch it alternate.

Then write the retry loop in Python (starter 03).

item.name: E2b  force a failure with X-Chaos  -> 503

request.description:
The X-Chaos header forces the outcome, so you can test your
retry logic against a guaranteed failure instead of waiting for
a random one. Change it to `pass` to force success.

A deliberately tight budget: a handful of calls per 30 seconds.

Keep hitting Send until you get 429, then look at Retry-After.
The server is telling you exactly how long to wait -- a good
client reads that rather than guessing.

Also note x-ratelimit-remaining on the successful responses: you
can see it coming and slow down before being blocked.
